stories.title: A landslide at a landfill in the capital of Guinea kills 30 people, officials say
stories.summary:
A landslide at a major landfill in Conakry, the capital of Guinea, killed at least 30 people early Sunday, according to an updated toll released by the central government.

The collapse occurred when heavy rains washed over the site, triggering a massive slide of refuse that buried several nearby homes and shacks. The incident took place at the largest landfill in the country's capital.

Rescue teams have launched a search for survivors as they work to clear the debris from the affected area.

stories.title: Trade war escalates after U.S.-Canada negotiations collapse
stories.summary:
Trade tensions between the United States and Canada have intensified following the collapse of bilateral negotiations. President Donald Trump indicated he would not compromise on the terms that led Canadian negotiators to walk away from the talks.

In a late-night social media post, Trump accused Canada of seeking the benefits of being a U.S. state while maintaining its own policies. The remarks signaled a hardline stance as the dispute over trade terms deepened.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by announcing retaliatory tariffs, which he described as a reluctant measure. Carney also accused the United States of initiating the current trade war.

stories.title: Once Australia's northern capital, Newcastle Waters became a ghost town
stories.summary:
Newcastle Waters, a remote settlement in the Northern Territory, is now remembered as a ghost town that briefly served as Australia's northern capital. A century ago, politicians in Canberra divided the territory and designated the isolated community as the seat of a new jurisdiction called North Australia.

The unusual arrangement has faded from public memory, but local history enthusiasts are working to preserve the story. They aim to ensure this quirky chapter of outback history is not forgotten.

stories.title: Seven First Nations Australians tell us their worries and hopes for future generations – video
stories.summary:
Seven First Nations Australians share their worries and hopes for future generations in a new video from The Guardian Australia.

The piece highlights East Arnhem Land, described as one of the last strongholds of Aboriginal culture in Australia. It is home to the Yolngu people, who maintain one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth.

The land is fully owned and managed by traditional owners under inalienable Aboriginal freehold title, meaning it can never be bought or sold.

Each year, the Yolngu host the Garma festival, described as Australia's largest Indigenous political and cultural gathering. The event brings together First Nations leaders from around the country.

The legality of training artificial intelligence models on copyrighted books remains an unsettled legal question. The issue has gained attention as many published authors have unknowingly contributed to the development of AI tools that may threaten their livelihoods.

While it might seem illegal for companies to use copyrighted works without knowledge or consent, the actual legal landscape is more complicated than a simple violation. TechCrunch notes that determining whether such practices constitute copyright infringement involves nuanced interpretations of existing laws rather than clear-cut prohibitions.

The dispute highlights growing tensions between legacy media institutions and digital-native creators. While proponents argue that algorithmic adjustments can ensure fair competition, influencers contend that such measures would entrench existing power structures at their expense.

Originally scheduled for Tuesday, August 25, the Simultaneous School Safety Drill will now take place during the first week of September 2026. This delay follows a separate push by two psychiatric groups urging the postponement of such simulations.

The Philippine Psychiatric Association and the Philippine Society for Child and Adolescent Psychiatry argued that current evidence does not show these drills reduce casualties or prevent incidents.

stories.title: Habagat to bring rain in Northern, Central Luzon areas Monday (Aug. 24)
stories.summary:
The southwest monsoon, or habagat, is expected to bring rain to parts of Northern and Central Luzon on Monday, August 24. The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (Pagasa) issued the forecast in its 5 a.m. weather update.

A Pagasa specialist noted that Typhoon Saudel and Tropical Depression conditions are also part of the broader weather picture affecting the region.

stories.title: U.N. and Congolese Troops Struggle to Halt Lightning Rebel Attack
stories.summary:
United Nations and Congolese forces are struggling to stop a rapid offensive by the Rwandan-backed M23 rebel group in eastern Congo. The rebels have captured two strategic towns on the approaches to Goma over the past several days.

Aid workers estimate that as many as 300,000 people are fleeing the advancing M23 forces. The situation has created a significant humanitarian crisis in the region.

stories.title: US battery startups have found a lifeline in defense
stories.summary:
U.S. battery startups have secured a significant financial boost amid industry challenges.

The Department of Energy awarded $500 million in grants to the sector, providing critical support after recent reductions in electric vehicle incentives left many companies struggling.

This funding is described as a lifeline for an industry that had been on the ropes due to shifting policy landscapes and reduced consumer subsidies.

links.headline: US battery startups have found a lifeline in defense
links.excerpt: U.S. battery startups pulled in $500 million in grants from the Department of Energy, throwing a lifeline to an industry that was on the ropes after EV incentives were slashed.

stories.title: A timely warning on the rise of the ‘tech bros’ from the author of The Nerd Reich | Letter
stories.summary:
Catherine Austin Fitts has written to The Guardian in support of journalist Gil Durán’s critique of Silicon Valley culture. In a letter responding to an interview with the author of “The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy,” Fitts argues that society must reject what she describes as the limited vision of the tech industry.

Fitts frames the issue as requiring more than policy changes, suggesting instead a broader shift in public consciousness. She aligns with Durán’s warning about the influence of “tech bros” and emphasizes the urgency of addressing their growing power over democratic institutions.

stories.title: Trump Says He Wants to 'Clean Out' Gaza, Send Refugees to Egypt and Jordan
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said he wants to “clean out” Gaza and send its refugees to Egypt and Jordan. He described the heavily bombed enclave as a “demotion site.”

The president proposed relocating Palestinians either temporarily or long-term. Arab countries have rejected such a move since the war began.

stories.title: Kim Jong Un Is Doing Everything He Can to Keep North Korea's Youth in Line
stories.summary:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un is intensifying efforts to control the country's youth by mobilizing them for state-directed labor. The regime has drafted approximately 300,000 teenagers and young adults into a "shock brigade" tasked with flood reconstruction work.

This initiative appears designed to counteract the cultural influence of Hollywood and K-pop, which authorities view as threats to ideological conformity. By exalting these young workers in state media, Kim seeks to reinforce loyalty while keeping the population insulated from external cultural trends.

links.headline: Kim Jong Un Is Doing Everything He Can to Keep North Korea's Youth in Line
links.excerpt: The dictator, eager to shut out the influence of Hollywood and K-pop, has been exalting a “shock brigade” of 300,000 teens and 20-somethings drafted into flood reconstruction.
